t: A carbon atom in your hand today was in the air last year, and in a rock for a hundred million years before that.
Carbon does not get used up. The atoms in you have been through air, ocean, plants, animals and rock, repeatedly, and they will go round again after you.
sub: Nothing is ever thrown away. There is nowhere to throw it.
Energy flows through and is lost. Matter has nowhere to go, so it cycles.

question: Where does the carbon go when you burn coal?
What is the fate of carbon released by combustion?
options: Into the air, and then into the ocean and plants over time
It is destroyed by the fire
stages.outcome: Into the air, and then into the ocean and plants over time
note: Commit. Atoms are not created or destroyed by burning — the question is only where they end up and how fast.

stages.label: How long does carbon stay there?
captions: In a leaf: weeks to months.
In the deep ocean: about a thousand years.
In rock and fossil fuel: hundreds of millions of years.
t: The same atom moves between all of these. Only the speed changes.
Residence time varies across nine orders of magnitude between reservoirs. That spread is what makes the cycle interesting rather than the fact of cycling.
after: Fast stores and slow stores, and burning coal moves carbon from the slowest to the fastest.

The transfer that matters is between reservoirs with very different residence times: fossil carbon locked away for a hundred million years is returned to the atmosphere in a moment, and the slow route back takes far longer than the release did.

t: Carbon going round between air, living things, oceans and rock is the carbon cycle.
The carbon cycle: exchange between atmosphere, biosphere, ocean and geological reservoirs, each with its own residence time.
A fast biological cycle turning over in years sits inside a slow geological one turning over in hundreds of millions. They are coupled, and the rate difference is the point.

Photosynthesis and respiration alone move roughly 120 gigatonnes of carbon a year each way and very nearly cancel. Against that enormous balanced flux, the human contribution of about 10 gigatonnes a year is small — and it does not cancel, which is why a small number changes the total and the large ones do not.
sub: Energy flows through and is lost. Matter goes round and round.
That is the difference worth holding: energy makes one pass from the sun to space, and matter has nowhere to leave to.
So there is no 'away'. Anything released is somewhere, and the only question is which reservoir and for how long.

The ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter of what has been released, which slowed the atmospheric rise and acidified the surface ocean by about 0.1 pH units — a 30% increase in hydrogen ion concentration. It is the clearest case of a sink not being a disposal.

q: Why is burning coal different from a tree rotting?
Both release CO₂. Why are they treated differently?
Why does fossil carbon count differently from biological carbon?
options: The coal's carbon had been out of circulation for a hundred million years
Coal makes a different kind of carbon dioxide
There is no difference at all
why: A rotting tree gives back carbon it took from the air a few decades ago, so it goes round in a circle. Coal's carbon was put away before the dinosaurs, and burning it adds to the circle instead of going round it.

The molecule is identical; the reservoir is not. Biological carbon cycles within the fast pool on a timescale of years, so it roughly balances. Fossil carbon is a transfer from the slow pool into the fast one, and nothing returns it at a comparable rate.

It is a question of flux balance rather than chemistry. The fast cycle's enormous fluxes very nearly cancel; a comparatively small one-way transfer from the geological reservoir does not, and it is the net that accumulates. The isotopic signature confirms the source directly — fossil carbon is depleted in ¹³C and contains no ¹⁴C, and atmospheric CO₂ shows both changes.

t: It is why planting trees helps, and why it is not a complete answer.

A growing tree genuinely removes carbon from the air and holds it. But it holds it in the fast pool — for decades, until the tree burns or rots — while fossil carbon came from a pool measured in hundreds of millions of years. Forests are a real and worthwhile sink, and they are not the same size or the same permanence as the source. Both halves of that are true and both get left out depending on who is talking.
